issues.title: SSO token expiry leaves client in stale "Connected" state — requires manual disconnect/reconnect to re-authenticate
issues.body:
**Describe the problem**

When the SSO session (Azure AD OpenID Connect) expires, the NetBird client remains in a "Connected" state (Management: Connected, Signal: Connected) but peer connectivity silently degrades. Some peers show as "Connecting" indefinitely and traffic no longer flows to them, while the client never triggers a re-authentication prompt.

The only workaround is to manually run netbird down followed by netbird up, which triggers a new SSO login flow and restores full connectivity.

This makes the client unreliable for long-running machines (servers, CI runners, etc.) where no user is around to notice the silent failure and manually cycle the connection.

**To Reproduce**

1. Set up a self-hosted NetBird deployment with Azure AD OpenID Connect as the identity provider.
2. Connect a client via netbird up and complete the SSO login.
3. Wait for the SSO/OAuth token to expire (depends on Azure AD token lifetime policy).
4. Observe that netbird status still shows Management: Connected and Signal: Connected, but traffic through netbird doesn't work
5. Run netbird down && netbird up — SSO re-authentication is triggered and all peers reconnect normally.

**Expected behavior**

When the SSO token expires, the client should either:

- Automatically refresh the token using a refresh token (if available), or
- Detect the expired/invalid session and trigger a re-authentication flow automatically, or
- Surface a clear status change (e.g., "Needs Login" / "Session Expired")

On a self-hosted deployment, `netbird up --foreground-mode` grew to **6.0 GB RSS**

The client did not exit, back off to a steady state, or cap its retry cost. It
kept allocating until the host ran out of memory and the kernel/init OOM killer
began terminating unrelated workloads on the same machine.

The memory is released immediately and completely on restart: a freshly started

issues.title: Support multiple identity connectors mapping to a single user account (native + OIDC merge)
issues.body:
**Component:** `management/server` — user identity model

### Summary

NetBird's embedded IdP (`/oauth2`, dex-compatible) supports multiple connectors: a `local` email/password connector and OIDC connectors (e.g., an external Pocket-ID / Keycloak / Auth0 IdP). When the same human authenticates through two different connectors, the management server creates **two separate user accounts**, because a user is keyed by `(identity, connector)`.

### Current behavior

Both rows are the same person (same email), but NetBird exposes two users. Peers attach to a single account, so the other login path appears to "lose" all devices. The only current remedy is the one-way `migration_up` tool (`management/server/idp/migration`, `MigrateUsersToStaticConnectors` / `UpdateUserID`), which:

* Is destructive / one-way — after re-keying, the native connector no longer maps to the account
* Re-keys **all** users, not a single user
* Removes the ability to use the native connector as a break-glass fallback

### Requested behavior

* Link multiple connector identities to a single user account, so the same person can log in via the native/local connector (break-glass) **or** an OIDC connector, resolving to the same NetBird user + peers.
* Provide an admin API/flow to **merge two existing users** (same email, different connector) non-destructively, without re-keying the whole account.
* Make `migration_up` optional rather than required.

issues.title: Group selector blocks the main thread ~190 ms per keystroke with ~960 groups (no list virtualization)
issues.body:
## Summary

On an account with **959 groups**, the group selector on the peer detail page renders **every group as
real DOM nodes** — no virtualization — and re-scores the full list on every keystroke. Opening the
selector adds **~20,700 DOM nodes** and blocks the main thread for **637 ms**; each subsequent
keystroke blocks it for a further **~190 ms**. Typing a 7-character filter costs **2.24 s of
cumulative main-thread blocking**, and every keystroke registers as a `longtask`.

Critically, **narrowing the query does not reduce the cost** — a query matching only **2** groups still
blocks for **323 ms**, because the work scales with the *total* number of groups, not the number of
results. There is therefore no way for an operator to type around this.

The server is not involved: `GET /api/groups` returns in ~260 ms (of which the database is ~7 ms), and
**no network request is made while typing** (verified: 0 new resource entries across 5 keystrokes).

# Generated password modal flashes and disappears when creating a user from an empty group's detail page

## Summary

On self-hosted with the embedded IdP, creating a user via **Access Control → Groups → *(group)* → Add User → Create User** shows the "User created successfully!" modal containing the generated password for a fraction of a second, then it vanishes before the password can be read or copied.

The user account *is* created successfully — but its password is displayed exactly once, and once lost there is no recovery path from the dashboard: the account is dead and must be **deleted and re-created**.

issues.title: Publish dashboard image to GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io)
issues.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

When self-hosting NetBira**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

When self-hosting NetBird, four of the five images that make up the
stack `netbird`, `management`, `signal`, `relay` are published on
GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io/netbirdio/...`). The dashboard is
the only one that lives exclusively on Docker Hub.

This split causes a few small but recurring annoyances for self-hosters:

- **Renovate (and similar bots) can't surface release notes for the
  dashboard.** Because GHCR images are tied to their GitHub repo,
  Renovate automatically attaches the matching release notes to every
  update PR for the four other components. The dashboard, coming from
  Docker Hub, has no such link its update PRs land "naked", with
  just a version bump and no changelog context. So out of five
  NetBird images, four PRs are informative and one is silent.

- **No unified release view for the stack.** If everything were on
  GHCR under `netbirdio`, self-hosters could follow a single coherent
  release timeline for the whole NetBird stack on GitHub. Today, the
  dashboard's release notes have to be tracked separately, on a
  different platform.

- **Inconsistent registry pinning.** It is currently impossible to
  keep the whole NetBird stack on a single registry, which complicates
  internal mirrors, firewall whitelists, and avoiding Docker Hub
  rate-limit headaches.
